title: the Rudram
hook: the hymn leaves the page and goes into the temple, where it is chanted while water pours over the stone
tomorrow: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Rudram's companion asked: cha me, and to me, right down to grain and a shared meal. Today is our last day inside the hymn.

A small brass pot hangs on a chain above a stone linga. There's a pinhole in its base, and water drips, one drop and then the next, onto the stone. In some Shiva temples that drip is kept going through the day. On festival days it grows louder: priests sit close around the linga, and while water and milk are poured over it, they chant. One of the hymns they may chant is the Rudram. It was never only something to read. It's something to pour to. Today we follow it out of the book and into the bath.
screen: `A POT, A PINHOLE, A STONE.` → `PRIESTS CHANT AS THE WATER POURS.` → `OUT OF THE BOOK, INTO THE BATH.`

segments.voice: The bath is called abhisheka, and when the Rudram is chanted with it, people call the rite Rudrabhisheka. Hold the hymn next to the water and its shape shows. It opens by bowing to Rudra's anger, his arrow, his bow and his arms, and asks that the arrow be turned away and the bow unstrung. Then it keeps bowing, and finds Rudra everywhere: in forest and field, among carpenters and chariot-makers, even, startlingly, as the lord of thieves. Nothing is left outside the bow. Deep inside comes the line namah shivaya cha shivataraya cha: salutation to the kind one, and to the one kinder still. A traditional saying goes: the Rudram sits at the heart of the Vedas, the five syllables namah shivaya at the heart of the Rudram, and the two syllables shi-va at the heart of those five. Take it as a picture, not a measurement. The movement is real either way: from a god with a drawn bow, inward, toward a name that means auspicious, gentle, kind. The water makes the same movement. Another old saying: Vishnu loves to be adorned, Shiva loves to be bathed. The one with fire in his third eye and poison held in his throat is offered coolness, again and again. Hymn and pouring do one job: they meet the frightening edge of things with a bow, one drop at a time, until it shows a kind face.
screen: `ABHISHEKA: THE SACRED BATH.` · `IT OPENS WITH RUDRA'S ANGER.` · `SHIVA SITS AT ITS HEART.` · `SHIVA LOVES TO BE BATHED.` · then, large: `TO THE KIND ONE, AND KINDER STILL.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing that feels fierce right now, a worry, a person, a deadline with its bow drawn, and without fighting or fixing it, picture cool water poured slowly over it on each out-breath. Let the thing stay what it is, and just keep pouring. If you pray, you can say namah shivaya softly with each pour, or the name of God you use.
The Rudram. A Vedic hymn that bows to the fierce Rudra again and again, until Shiva, the kind one, appears at its heart. Today, chanted while the water pours.
Your line: the Rudram. Tomorrow, a great night of Shiva. See you then.

howItsDone: In Shiva temples and in homes, Hindus may chant the Rudram during abhisheka, pouring water, milk and other offerings over the linga; some families arrange a Rudrabhisheka for a festival, a new home, or a hard time.

notes: Last of the Rudram days (1146–1152). Review picks up 1151 (the chamakam, cha me). 1146–1151 covered the opening to Rudra's anger, the sun, namah, the short and tall, trees and foam, and the chamakam; this day takes the hymn into abhisheka and the namah shivaya line, recalling the opening only briefly.

Confirm: the dripping vessel (dhara patra) over the linga in some Shiva temples; 'Rudrabhisheka' as the name of the rite; the opening of the namakam (namaste rudra manyava...) paraphrased as bowing to anger, arrow, bow and arms and asking that the arrow be turned away.

Confirm the namakam's salutations to the lord of thieves (stenanam pataye / taskaranam pataye) and to carpenters and chariot-makers (takshabhyo rathakarebhyash cha), and the gloss of shivataraya as 'kinder still / more auspicious'.
The 'heart of the Vedas' saying (Rudram > Panchakshara > shi-va) is presented as a traditional saying and 'a picture, not a measurement'; confirm wording and that it is not mis-attributed.
'Alankara priyo vishnuh, abhisheka priyah shivah' paraphrased as an old saying; confirm.
Practice invites saying 'namah shivaya' with each breath, an existing mantra, not a new prayer.
